sources.title: UNESCO: Bahla Fort
sources.note: Official statement of outstanding universal value: Banu Nebhan capital and central Omani power from the twelfth to late fifteenth centuries; Ibadi setting, earthen fort, oasis and falaj. Read directly. Surviving settlement descriptions do not date every building to the medieval period.

sources.title: UNESCO: Ancient City of Qalhat
sources.note: Official listing, history and trade connections. Read directly. Qalhat is a separate port near Sur, not Muscat. General eleventh to sixteenth century prosperity is not treated as a precise founding date or uninterrupted Hormuzi sovereignty.

sources.title: Ibn Battuta: Rihla, part two, return journey through Muscat
sources.note: Modern Hindawi Arabic edition, redirecting to safahat.org. Direct HTML paragraph beginning ثم ركبت البحر فوصلت إلى مسقط, corresponding to printed page 469 of the downloadable edition (PDF page 469). Preceding itinerary dates return journey to 748 AH, 1347 CE. Three-word witness فوصلت إلى مسقط verified in text extraction; translation is our close translation. Modern typeset text, not a local inscription or surviving fourteenth-century manuscript.

sources.title: Oman Ministry of Heritage and Culture: Qalhat nomination dossier (2017)
sources.note: Official nomination, indexed original text: historical account of Bibi Maryam; printed page 34 sections 2.c.3 Hammam, 2.c.4 Water Infrastructure and 2.c.5 Domestic Buildings. Direct document fetch failed; substantive indexed passages read. Bath excavated partly in 2003. B2 cistern dimensions 13.70 by 4.10 by 5.10 m, capacity over 280 cubic metres. Avoid inconsistent AH/CE date conversion in dossier. B94 has adjoining houses without an internal connection.

sources.title: Axelle Rougeulle: Qalhat, a Medieval Port City of Oman (2023), publisher sample
sources.note: Original excavation director book; publisher sample read directly. Printed page 2 describes 1998 underwater survey and more than twenty stone anchors; printed pages 7 to 8 describe pottery workshop, chemical analysis, sampling and flotation, plus photogrammetry. Sample only, not a claim to reading the full book.

sources.title: Dabrowski, Marrast, Monchot and Rougeulle: Rice, lamb and tuna (2024)
sources.note: Original Archaeological Research in Asia 40, 100561, DOI 10.1016/j.ara.2024.100561. Indexed original abstract and section previews read; direct fetch denied. B94 spatial food study, open-water fishing, oasis provisioning and caprine predominance among identified terrestrial animal remains. Hypothesized room activities kept qualified.

sources.title: Dabrowski and colleagues: Plant Supplying Strategies in an Islamic Omani Harbour City (2018)
sources.note: Journal of Islamic Archaeology 5(1), pages 17 to 38. Indexed publisher abstract and author-uploaded paper excerpts, especially pages 30 to 32, read. B39 workshop, fourteenth to sixteenth centuries: crop processing in room E; rice, finger millet, pulses and sesame; local cultivation versus import remains debated. Full DOI fetch unavailable.

sources.title: Ana Lopes and Jorge Correia: Portuguese fortifications in Muscat (2017)
sources.note: University research record and full original abstract read. Genius Loci volume 2, pages 219 to 230; Muscat Portuguese period 1507 to 1650, harbour setting and interdependent Al Jalali and Al Mirani defenses. Does not establish all surviving fabric as present in 1507.

sources.title: Ermertz and colleagues: Geoarchaeological Evidence for the Decline of Qalhat (2019)
sources.note: Original Open Quaternary 5(8), pages 1 to 14, repository abstract read directly. Geological fieldwork and digital elevation model support earthquake activity as a plausible contributor to decline, not proof of a precisely dated destructive event.

sources.title: Ras Al Khaimah Department of Antiquities and Museums: European interest
sources.note: Official museum historical account read directly: Ya’aruba expulsion of Portuguese from Julfar and Dibba in 1633, Sohar in 1643 and Muscat in 1650. Used only for this later dated transition.

proposedOverrides.name: Muscat
proposedOverrides.summary: Medieval Muscat within the varied political and trading world of coastal and inland Oman.

batchIdentityNotes.scope: Eight imported polygons cover northern and eastern Oman and substantial inland areas, with the last two extending west to about 50.568 E. They are not the limits of Muscat town or evidence for a continuous Muscat kingdom. Public opening makes this explicit.
batchIdentityNotes.related: Separate indexed oman 1530 to 1914 and muscat-and-oman 1938 to 1945 remain unassociated. Qalhat and Bahla are explicitly located comparative regional centres, not aliases of Muscat.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Ibn Battuta Arabic travel account, modern edition, return journey 1347; exact short witness verified as text, no claim of visual manuscript verification.
